Download the current 64-bit Windows installer unless your computer specifically requires another build. Record the ProteoWizard version used for conversion because conversion software is part of the analysis provenance.

title: RAW → mzML on Windows
text:
Install on Windows
Run the installer and keep the standard MSConvert components. The current ProteoWizard Windows installer documentation requires Microsoft .NET Framework 4.7.2 or newer.
After installation, you should have:

MSConvertGUI for graphical conversion;
msconvert.exe for command-line conversion;
SeeMS for inspecting open-format spectra.

A typical installation is inside a versioned directory under:
C:\Program Files\ProteoWizard\
The exact subdirectory depends on the installed build.

Verify the installation
Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and run:
msconvert.exe --help
If the command is not found, either run msconvert.exe using its full path or add the ProteoWizard installation directory to PATH.

title: RAW → mzML on Windows
text:
Convert with MSConvertGUI
The annotated screenshot below shows the six PXD065315 control RAW files. The three red markers indicate the core workflow: 1 choose the RAW files, 2 select mzML, and 3 start conversion.






Figure 1: MSConvertGUI example for converting the six PXD065315 control RAW files to mzML. Red markers indicate the main sequence: select the RAW files, choose mzML as the output format, and click Start.




1. Add RAW files
Click Browse and add one or more vendor RAW files. Convert all samples in one batch whenever possible so they receive identical settings.
For the ProtVis PXD065315 control example:
B73_C1.raw
B73_C2.raw
B73_C3.raw
EA2024_C1.raw
EA2024_C2.raw
EA2024_C3.raw


2. Use a separate output directory
Do not mix converted mzML files with the original RAW files. For example:
E:\count\p_raw\      # original RAW
E:\count\p_mzML\     # converted mzML
Select E:\count\p_mzML\ as the Output Directory.


3. Set the output format
Use:
Output format: mzML
Leave Package in gzip off because ProtVis expects ordinary .mzML filenames in the current Raw workflow.


4. Keep zlib compression enabled
Recommended:
Write index: enabled
Use zlib compression: enabled
Binary encoding precision: 64-bit
zlib reduces file size without changing the numerical spectra. Numpress options are not required for this workflow and can remain disabled unless they are part of a validated pipeline.


5. Decide whether Peak Picking is required
If the RAW file contains profile-mode spectra that should be centroided before Sage searching, add the Peak Picking filter. For Thermo data, use vendor peak picking when available and place Peak Picking first in the filter list.
A commonly used command-line equivalent is:
peakPicking true 1-
This means peak picking from MS1 upward.






WarningDo not centroid twice



If the acquisition is already centroided, do not add Peak Picking simply because the option exists. Redundant centroiding can unnecessarily alter the spectra. Confirm the acquisition mode before conversion.




6. Choose a reasonable parallel file count
For a six-file conversion, 2–4 files in parallel is usually a safer starting point than launching all files simultaneously. Conversion can be disk-I/O and memory intensive.


7. Start conversion
Click Start and wait until all files complete without errors. The output filename stems should remain unchanged:
B73_C1.raw     → B73_C1.mzML
B73_C2.raw     → B73_C2.mzML
EA2024_C1.raw  → EA2024_C1.mzML

title: RAW → mzML on Windows
text:
Convert from the command line

One file
msconvert.exe "E:\count\p_raw\B73_C1.raw" --mzML --zlib --filter "peakPicking true 1-" -o "E:\count\p_mzML"


All RAW files in a directory
msconvert.exe "E:\count\p_raw\*.raw" --mzML --zlib --filter "peakPicking true 1-" -o "E:\count\p_mzML"
If the data are already centroided, omit the Peak Picking filter:
msconvert.exe "E:\count\p_raw\*.raw" --mzML --zlib -o "E:\count\p_mzML"
Inspect the exact options provided by the installed build with:
msconvert.exe --help
msconvert.exe --show-examples

title: RAW → mzML on Windows
text:
Troubleshooting
MSConvert cannot read a RAW file. Confirm that the file is complete, the correct vendor reader is available, and conversion is being performed with a current Windows ProteoWizard installation.
The mzML files are unexpectedly huge. Confirm that zlib compression is enabled. Profile-mode data can also be much larger than centroided data.
Sage finds very few or no PSMs. First verify that the mzML contains valid MS2 spectra and that centroiding was appropriate. Then check FASTA, enzyme, modifications, precursor tolerance and fragment tolerance.
ProtVis reports files as missing. sample_info$mzml_file must exactly match the converted filename, including .mzML.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Open Search → FragPipe when a Raw project needs a more comprehensive search workflow than the lightweight Sage route. ProtVis uses the official FragPipe runtime and its headless interface; it does not redistribute separately licensed FragPipe companion binaries inside the R package.
The Raw route is:
Project init → Search → FragPipe → Project Dashboard → Pre-processing
FragPipe can work with compatible LC-MS inputs registered in Project init, including mzML/mzXML and, when the official runtime supports them, vendor RAW, MGF or .d inputs.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Prerequisites
Before opening Search:

Set a writable project directory.
Upload sample information with sample_id plus a file column such as mzml_file, raw_file or filename.
Upload the protein FASTA.
Select the LC-MS input directory and click Check LC-MS files.
Select Raw and run Project init.

Unlike Sage, FragPipe is not bundled into ProtVis because the complete FragPipe ecosystem contains components with separate licenses. ProtVis instead detects an existing official runtime or helps obtain the official platform release at runtime.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Runtime detection and installation
The FragPipe panel reports the status of FragPipe/version, workflows, tools folder, MSFragger, IonQuant, diaTracer, DIA-NN, Java and Python. Use Refresh after changing a path. If FragPipe is not detected, use Install FragPipe or provide the installation path manually.






Note



On macOS, the current integration reports official FragPipe support as Docker/headless. Configure a compatible Docker/headless wrapper rather than assuming a native desktop installation is available.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Workflow presets
ProtVis exposes official presets including LFQ + MBR, Basic search, LFQ phosphoproteomics, Open search, Quick open search, TMT10 phosphoproteomics, DIA spectral library + quantification, and DIA phosphoproteomics. A custom .workflow file can also be supplied.
Choose the preset that matches the acquisition design. Workflow selection is part of the search model and should be recorded.

title: FragPipe search
text:
What ProtVis prepares
Before launching headless FragPipe, ProtVis resolves the runtime, prepares the workflow, writes the project FASTA into the workflow configuration, writes a no-header manifest from registered LC-MS files/sample metadata, creates FragPipe_search, and records runtime versions, parameters and file fingerprints.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Run FragPipe
Review workflow, data type, threads, RAM and optional runtime paths. Advanced workflows can also require Python or DIA-NN. Use FragPipe dry run when you want to validate the generated command/workflow without completing the search.
Click Run FragPipe Search once. The result area provides QC Summary, PSMs, Peptides, Proteins, Files, the FragPipe log and the runtime-component table. The status panel reports parsed PSM, peptide and protein row counts.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Handoff to ProtVis_dataset
ProtVis stores the search bundle in the active project and registers PSM/peptide assays in schema v4. A compatible protein report is harmonized into the canonical protein-by-sample matrix so later modules use the same ProtVis_dataset interface as Sage or tabular imports.
Search provenance includes workflow, manifest, runtime versions, input/output fingerprints, parameters and log. Re-running a search creates a new recorded run instead of silently replacing previous analytical history.
After a successful search, inspect Project Dashboard before continuing.

title: FragPipe search
text:
Script entry points
ProtVis::protvis_fragpipe_status()
ProtVis::protvis_install_fragpipe()
ProtVis::protvis_fragpipe_workflow_presets()

result <- ProtVis::run_fragpipe_search(
  fasta = "proteins.fasta",
  spectra_paths = list.files("spectra", full.names = TRUE),
  output_directory = "FragPipe_search",
  workflow = "LFQ + MBR"
)
The same backend is available from the Headless / CLI workflow.






Warning



Preserve the exact workflow file, manifest, FASTA and runtime version used for the final result.

title: Plant-mPLoc
text:
Toolkits → Plant-mPLoc predicts plant-protein subcellular localization from an amino-acid sequence. ProtVis submits the sequence to the public Plant-mPLoc academic server and parses one or more predicted cellular locations.
The current integration recognizes 12 location classes, including chloroplast, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion, cell membrane, cell wall, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, extracellular space, peroxisome, plastid and vacuole.

title: Plant-mPLoc
text:
Input
Enter a Protein ID and a complete protein sequence using the 20 standard one-letter amino-acid codes. Whitespace is removed automatically and non-standard characters are rejected.
Click LOAD DEMO SEQUENCE to test the module with the bundled plant-protein sequence.

title: Plant-mPLoc
text:
Advanced settings
The module exposes Timeout (seconds), default 90, and Allow the legacy server certificate, enabled by default.






Warning



Disabling certificate verification reduces transport security. Use it only for this legacy academic endpoint when normal validation fails, and do not submit confidential sequences to a service you do not trust.

title: Plant-mPLoc
text:
Run the prediction
Click PREDICT LOCALIZATION. The result area reports status, protein ID/sequence length, number of predicted locations, prediction badges, result table, raw server response and method/publication information.
Use DOWNLOAD RESULT to save the parsed prediction as CSV.

title: Plant-mPLoc
text:
External-service limitation
Plant-mPLoc is not executed locally. Internet access and the availability/layout of the external server are required. If the server changes its HTML form or result page, ProtVis may receive a page but fail to identify the prediction. The Raw response tab is useful for troubleshooting.

title: Plant-mPLoc
text:
Programmatic use
res <- ProtVis::predict_plant_mploc(
  sequence = my_sequence,
  id = "ZmProtein",
  timeout = 90,
  ignore_ssl = TRUE
)

res$prediction
When an active ProtVis_dataset exists, the GUI records the prediction as a schema-v4 analysis run with the protein ID, settings and result table.

The module accepts an Excel table in wide format, where each selected column represents one group.

title: Boxplot
text: Use Toolkits → Boxplot to compare quantitative values among multiple groups, display the underlying observations, add statistical annotations, and export both the figure and the statistical results. The module accepts an Excel table in wide format, where each selected column represents one group.

title: Boxplot
text:
Boxplot interface
The screenshot below shows the bundled demonstration data with three groups (Group_A, Group_B, and Group_C). The example contains six observations per group. The visible pairwise p-values and significance symbols belong only to this demonstration dataset.






Figure 1: ProtVis Boxplot interface showing demo-data loading, group selection, pairwise comparisons, plot parameters, a three-group boxplot and the statistical-results table.

title: Boxplot
text:
Input format
Upload a .xlsx table in wide format. Each quantitative group should occupy one column:
Group_A  Group_B  Group_C
5.1      6.1      7.0
5.4      6.5      7.2
5.0      6.0      6.9
5.3      6.3      7.4
5.6      6.4      7.1
5.2      6.2      7.3
This is also the structure of the current built-in demonstration data. After group selection, ProtVis reshapes the selected columns into Group and Value fields. Missing values are removed; values that cannot be converted to numeric are also excluded from plotting and statistical analysis.

title: Boxplot
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load the data. Under Data Input, upload an Excel .xlsx file or click LOAD DEMO DATA. Demo data are provided so the complete workflow can be tested without preparing a file first.
2. Check Uploaded Data Preview. Confirm that the column names are the intended group names and that the quantitative values have been read correctly. In the demonstration screenshot the table contains Group_A, Group_B, and Group_C.
3. Select groups to display. Under Select groups, choose the columns that should be retained in the boxplot and analysis. The order of these selections is preserved as the group order in the plot.
4. Choose groups used for pairwise comparison. Groups used for pairwise comparison controls which groups enter the pairwise comparison set. When at least two groups are selected, ProtVis generates all pair combinations among those selected groups. This control is directly relevant to t.test and wilcox.test.
5. Select the statistical method. Open Statistics and choose one of the current methods:

t.test: pairwise t-tests for the selected comparison groups;
wilcox.test: pairwise Wilcoxon tests;
anova: one-way ANOVA followed by a TukeyHSD result table;
kruskal.test: overall Kruskal-Wallis test.

The current default is t.test.
6. Decide whether significance labels should appear on the plot. Keep Show significance labels on plot selected when statistical annotations are desired. Pairwise t-test/Wilcoxon analyses display pairwise significance labels, whereas ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis display an overall p-value.
7. Configure Plot Parameters. Set X-axis label and Y-axis label, adjust Box width and Point size, decide whether to Show data points, choose the box-line color, and set individual group fill colors. Showing individual points is recommended when sample size is modest because it makes the underlying observations visible instead of relying on the box summary alone.
8. Choose a theme. Available themes are minimal, classic, light, bw, dark, and grey. The current default is grey.
9. Click Run. ProtVis reshapes the selected groups, removes missing/non-numeric values, performs the selected statistical analysis, and generates the boxplot.
10. Review Statistical Results. For pairwise t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, the result table includes the compared groups, raw p, BH-adjusted p.adj, formatted values, significance symbols and method. In the screenshot, all three pairwise comparisons are significant because this is a deliberately separated demo dataset; those values are not reference thresholds for biological data.
11. Review ANOVA/Tukey or Kruskal output when those methods are selected. ANOVA produces an ANOVA Results table plus TukeyHSD Results. Kruskal-Wallis produces the overall test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value. The current Kruskal option is an overall test and does not automatically create a post-hoc pairwise table.
12. Export the figure and statistics. Under Download, choose pdf, png, jpg, or svg, set figure width and height, and set DPI for PNG/JPG output. Download Plot exports the current figure. Download Statistics writes an Excel workbook named like boxplot_statistics_YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx containing the available statistical result tables.

title: Boxplot
text:
Statistical behavior
For t.test and wilcox.test, ProtVis uses ggpubr::compare_means() across all pair combinations generated from the selected comparison groups. The statistical-results table uses Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) multiple-testing adjustment and exposes the adjusted p-value as p.adj.
For anova, ProtVis fits a one-way model:
Value ~ Group
and reports the ANOVA table together with TukeyHSD post-hoc comparisons. For kruskal.test, the current implementation reports the overall Kruskal-Wallis result.

title: Boxplot
text:
Interpreting the plot
The box represents the distribution summary for each group, while the optional jittered points show the individual observations. A small p-value indicates evidence against the null hypothesis under the selected test, but it does not by itself describe effect size or biological importance. Interpret the figure together with the group distributions, sample size and experimental design.






ImportantMatch the test to the experimental design



The current pairwise t-test/Wilcoxon workflow treats the groups as independent. Do not use it for paired or repeated-measures designs unless the statistical model correctly accounts for that structure. ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis likewise assume an appropriate independent-group design in the current module.








Tip



For figures intended for publication, keep the individual points visible when feasible and report the exact statistical test, multiple-testing correction, sample size and whether observations are independent or paired in the figure legend or Methods section.

title: Protein structure
text:
Use Toolkits → Protein Structure to analyze a protein structure from a .pdb file with ProtVis’s current bio3d workflow. The module reads the PDB structure, performs Normal Mode Analysis (NMA), plots residue-level fluctuations, overlays alpha-helix and beta-sheet annotations, and summarizes the loaded structure.
This module is different from Toolkits → SwissModel. SwissModel is used to generate or retrieve a predicted structure from a protein sequence; Protein Structure starts from an existing PDB file and performs structural fluctuation analysis.

title: Protein structure
text:
Use Toolkits → Protein Structure to analyze a protein structure from a .pdb file with ProtVis’s current bio3d workflow. The module reads the PDB structure, performs Normal Mode Analysis (NMA), plots residue-level fluctuations, overlays alpha-helix and beta-sheet annotations, and summarizes the loaded structure.
This module is different from Toolkits → SwissModel. SwissModel is used to generate or retrieve a predicted structure from a protein sequence; Protein Structure starts from an existing PDB file and performs structural fluctuation analysis.

title: Protein structure
text:
Protein Structure interface
The screenshot below shows the current Protein Structure interface. The left sidebar contains File Upload, Demo Data, Parameters, Run, and Download controls. The main area contains the Secondary Structure Plot and Structure Summary panels.






Figure 1: ProtVis Protein Structure interface showing PDB input, built-in demo data, NMA plotting parameters, export controls, the residue-fluctuation plot and the structure summary table.

title: Protein structure
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load a PDB structure. Under File Upload, upload a .pdb file. ProtVis validates the extension before accepting the file. Alternatively, open Demo Data and click Use Demo PDB to load the bundled 1hel.pdb example.
2. Confirm the active source. The Demo Data panel reports the current source and active file name. When the built-in example is selected, ProtVis immediately triggers the same analysis workflow used by the Run button.
3. Adjust the display parameters. Under Parameters, set Beta sheet color, Alpha helix color, and Line width. The current defaults use an orange beta-sheet color, a purple alpha-helix color, and a line width of 2.5.
4. Run the analysis. Click Run for an uploaded PDB file. If no file has been explicitly selected, the current implementation can fall back to the bundled demo PDB when it is available.
5. Inspect the Secondary Structure Plot. ProtVis reads the PDB with bio3d::read.pdb(), calculates normal modes with bio3d::nma(), and plots modes$fluctuations using bio3d::plot.bio3d(). The x-axis represents residue position and the y-axis represents Fluctuations from NMA. Secondary-structure information from the PDB is overlaid so helices and sheets can be interpreted together with the fluctuation profile.
6. Inspect the Structure Summary. The summary panel reports structural information derived from the parsed PDB, including structure size and available secondary-structure information. Use this panel to confirm that the intended structure was analyzed before interpreting the fluctuation plot.
7. Export the figure. Under Download, set plot width, height, units, resolution, and file format. ProtVis currently supports PDF, PNG, JPEG, TIFF, and SVG. PDF and SVG are vector outputs; PNG, JPEG, and TIFF use the selected DPI.

title: Protein structure
text:
What the plot represents
Normal Mode Analysis approximates collective motions that are accessible around the current protein conformation. In the ProtVis plot, larger residue-level fluctuation values indicate regions predicted to participate more strongly in these low-frequency motions, whereas lower values indicate comparatively constrained regions.
The secondary-structure overlay helps distinguish whether flexible or constrained regions correspond to alpha helices, beta sheets, or less structured segments. These patterns are useful for structural interpretation of domains, loops, mutation sites, PTMs, or candidate functional regions.

title: Protein structure
text:
Current ProtVis implementation
The core calculation follows the standard bio3d workflow:
pdb <- bio3d::read.pdb(pdb_file)
modes <- bio3d::nma(pdb)

bio3d::plot.bio3d(
  modes$fluctuations,
  sse = pdb,
  sheet.col = sheet_color,
  helix.col = helix_color,
  typ = "l",
  lwd = line_width,
  xlab = "Residue",
  ylab = "Fluctuations from NMA"
)
This means the plotted line is the NMA fluctuation profile itself rather than a generic abundance or confidence score.

title: Protein structure
text:
Input requirements
The uploaded file must be a valid protein .pdb file that can be parsed by bio3d and contains the structural atoms required for NMA. If the structure lacks suitable protein C-alpha atoms or cannot be processed by the normal-mode calculation, ProtVis reports an analysis failure rather than producing a misleading plot.






Tip



Use the bundled 1hel.pdb example first when checking a new installation. If the demo works but an uploaded structure fails, the issue is more likely to be the PDB content than the Protein Structure module itself.








Warning



Normal Mode Analysis is a model of collective structural motions, not a direct experimental measurement of residue dynamics. Interpret NMA together with the structure source, model quality, experimental evidence, domains, interfaces, and known functional sites.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Use Toolkits → Correlation chord to explore relationships among numeric traits, proteins, metabolites, pathways or other quantitative variables. ProtVis calculates a correlation matrix from selected columns, filters relationships by absolute correlation, retains the strongest links up to a user-defined maximum, and displays the result as a chord diagram.
This module is designed for a focused correlation network rather than for drawing every possible pair. Filtering keeps the diagram interpretable and makes the exact displayed relationships available as a table.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Correlation Chord interface
The screenshot below shows the built-in example containing eight variables: Root_length, Shoot_length, Fresh_weight, Dry_weight, Proline, Sodium, Potassium, and Chlorophyll. In this example the analysis uses Pearson correlation and an absolute correlation threshold of 0.6; the displayed link counts belong only to this demonstration dataset.






Figure 1: ProtVis Correlation Chord interface showing example phenotype variables, correlation matrix, selected links, analysis summary and chord diagram.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load a numeric dataset. Under Input Data, upload .csv, .tsv, or .txt, or click Use Example Data. The built-in example contains 48 observations for the eight variables shown in the screenshot.
2. Select the variables. Use Select Numeric Columns to choose at least two numeric columns. ProtVis automatically offers only numeric variables from the loaded table.
3. Choose the correlation method. Under Analysis Settings, select pearson, spearman, or kendall. Pearson is the current default. Pearson summarizes linear association, whereas rank-based Spearman or Kendall can be more appropriate for monotonic relationships or data that do not satisfy Pearson assumptions.
4. Set the Absolute Correlation Threshold. The default is 0.6. ProtVis retains a pair only when abs(correlation) >= threshold, so the same cutoff applies to positive and negative relationships.
5. Set Maximum Number of Links. The current control ranges from 10 to 200 and defaults to 50. After the threshold filter, ProtVis sorts relationships by absolute correlation from strongest to weakest and keeps at most this many links. This limit is especially important when many variables are selected.
6. Click Run. ProtVis calculates the correlation matrix using pairwise-complete observations, removes self-correlations, collapses the two directions of each variable pair into one link, applies the absolute-correlation threshold, and then applies the maximum-link limit.
7. Review the previews before interpreting the diagram. Uploaded Data Preview shows the source values, Correlation Matrix Preview shows the complete selected-variable matrix, and Selected Links Preview shows the exact filtered edges that are sent to the chord diagram.
8. Check Analysis Summary. The summary reports status, number of selected variables, total links shown, positive and negative link counts, threshold, and correlation method. This provides a compact record of the settings behind the displayed network.
9. Adjust Display Settings. Label Size changes variable-label size; Link Transparency controls visual opacity; Positive Correlation Color and Negative Correlation Color set the two link classes. The current defaults are red #D73027 for positive and blue #4575B4 for negative correlations.
10. Export the result. The Download section provides PDF and PNG versions of the chord diagram plus correlation_matrix.csv. Keep the matrix together with the figure so the exact numerical relationships remain available independently of the visualization.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Input format
A typical input table has observations in rows and numeric variables in columns:
Root_length,Shoot_length,Fresh_weight,Proline,Sodium
12.3,18.4,5.8,1.21,0.42
10.9,16.7,5.1,1.56,0.71

title: Correlation chord
text:
How links are selected
For the selected variables, ProtVis calls the correlation calculation with use = "pairwise.complete.obs". It then removes diagonal correlations and duplicate mirrored pairs such as A–B versus B–A. Pairs failing the absolute threshold are removed. The surviving pairs are ordered by |r| or the corresponding absolute rank-correlation coefficient, and only the strongest Maximum Number of Links are retained.
This means the chord diagram can intentionally show fewer relationships than the full correlation matrix. Use Selected Links Preview when you need the precise edge list represented in the figure.






WarningCorrelation is not causation



A strong chord indicates statistical association, not a causal relationship. For large correlation screens, also consider sample size, multiple testing, repeated-measures structure, and confounding variables before making biological conclusions.








Tip



If the diagram is crowded, increase the absolute-correlation threshold or reduce the maximum number of links rather than shrinking labels until the network becomes unreadable.

Background Maker interface

text:
Required input

GOs and KEGG_Pathway may contain multiple comma-separated annotations for one query sequence.

title: Background make
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Upload the eggNOG annotation file. In File Upload, choose the annotation table. After upload, the file information panel shows the selected filename and the current validation state.
2. Check the file before generating a background. Click Check File. ProtVis verifies that query, GOs, and KEGG_Pathway are present. Continue only when the status reports File format check passed. The Run Background Maker action is intended to be used after this validation step.
3. Set the Gene ID Separator. The default separator is _. ProtVis uses this character to extract the stable ID from the beginning of the query field. For example:
Zm00001eb321680_T001
with _ becomes:
Zm00001eb321680
Choose a separator that matches the identifier convention of the uploaded annotation. Do not use _ automatically when your IDs follow a different scheme.
4. Run Background Maker. Click Run Background Maker. ProtVis expands comma-separated GO terms, retrieves GO term names from GO.db, removes unresolved GO annotations, and creates distinct GENE, TERM, NAME records. For KEGG, it keeps pathway IDs matching the map##### form and obtains pathway names from the KEGG pathway list when available.
5. Review the summary cards. FILE STATUS confirms whether the source file passed validation. GO SUMMARY and KEGG SUMMARY report record counts, unique genes and unique terms. Large differences between the number of source genes and annotated genes are expected when some genes lack GO or KEGG assignments, but unexpected losses should be investigated.
6. Inspect both output tables. The GO Background and KEGG Background cards show the enrichment-ready records. Each table should contain:
GENE
TERM
NAME
Check a few known genes and pathways before using the workbook for enrichment analysis.
7. Download the background workbook. Click Download Background. ProtVis writes a file named like background_YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx containing three worksheets: Summary, GO_background, and KEGG_background. The Summary sheet records the uploaded file and the generated record/gene/term counts.
8. Use Example Data when learning the format. Example Data downloads background_maker_example_data.csv, which can be used as a minimal template for the three required source columns.

title: Background make
section: How GO and KEGG records are generated
text:
How GO and KEGG records are generated
For GO annotations, ProtVis separates the comma-delimited GOs field, removes missing or - entries, extracts the stable gene ID, maps each GO ID to its term name, removes terms that cannot be resolved, and de-duplicates the resulting records.
For KEGG, ProtVis separates KEGG_Pathway, keeps valid map pathway identifiers such as map01100, and resolves pathway names through the KEGG pathway-list service. If a pathway-name lookup is unavailable, the current implementation can retain the pathway ID itself as the name rather than discarding that valid mapping.






ImportantUse the correct enrichment universe



The background should represent the genes/proteins that could realistically have been detected or tested in the experiment. Do not build the background only from significant proteins; doing so changes the statistical universe and can distort enrichment results.








Tip



Keep the generated workbook together with the eggNOG source file and record the annotation/database version. This makes later enrichment results substantially easier to reproduce.

Lower technical dispersion or higher correlation can be useful, but they do not prove that a normalization preserves the biological signal. Choose a method based on acquisition type, scale, design and expected global biology, then record the method explicitly.

text:

Overview & QC — correlation, expression heatmap, archived UMAP reproduction, normalized intensity density and protein CV.

Pathview — project pathway-level effects onto KEGG maps.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
Recommended DEP versus complete-matrix analyses
Imputation and normalization remain valuable for visualization and methods that require a complete matrix. They are not automatically appropriate for hypothesis testing. Recommended DEP uses observed values, detection filtering and robust limma statistics so missing observations are not converted into artificial inferential evidence.
Presence/absence candidates—proteins observed repeatedly in only one comparison group—are retained as a parallel evidence stream rather than being forced into ordinary fold-change statistics.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
Reproduction modes
Some modules now have explicit historical-reproduction modes. These are intended to match archived manuscript figures/settings and should not be confused with the recommended default for a new experiment.






Important



Changing plot aesthetics does not change the model; changing the input matrix, detection filter, ranking metric, FDR/effect-size threshold or statistical engine does. Preserve these analysis settings in the schema-v4 run record and manuscript Methods.

text:

Downstream analyses append immutable runs to ProtVis_dataset. Tables, statistics, plot data/configuration, files and upstream dependencies are stored without overwriting previous executions. Re-running an upstream stage can invalidate downstream nodes while retaining their historical results.

title: Enrichment analysis
text:
Directional KEGG
The newer Directional KEGG tab is designed for the archived maize/teosinte Figure 3 enrichment logic. It separates directional DEP evidence, can load the archived comparison context, and calculates KEGG pathway enrichment from the supplied/bundled background rather than embedding a static pre-rendered result table.
The current layout provides selection/evidence controls, comparison/background settings, plot controls and configurable blue-gradient colors. The archived gene-membership support lives under inst/extdata/figure3_archive/ so the historical figure can be reproduced from the analysis inputs rather than from a stored picture.
Use this workspace when exact historical directional membership is the target. For a new dataset, use the standard enrichment tab unless the directional design is explicitly part of the analysis plan.






ImportantReproduction mode is not a new significance recommendation



The archived Figure 3 settings exist for reproducibility. Do not adopt its gene membership or presentation thresholds as generic defaults for another experiment.

Troubleshooting
Valid table but empty plot. Check term significance/filtering and confirm IDs match the background namespace.
No DEP list appears. Run/store DEP first or upload a gene list explicitly.
Pathways differ from an older figure. Confirm comparison direction, exact background database/version, DEP membership definition and whether the directional archived membership was selected.

title: GSEA
text:
Standard GSEA
Standard mode remains file-driven. Upload:

Expression Matrix (.txt);
Group Info (.txt);
KO Pathway Info (.txt).

The standard workflow builds a differential ranking and runs clusterProfiler::GSEA(). Current controls include minGSSize, maxGSSize, Top X pathways, significant-only (p.adjust < 0.05), NES/p.adjust sorting, and a selected pathway for the enrichment curve.
Because the standard ranking step uses count-model logic, do not supply already log-transformed continuous protein intensities as though they were integer counts.

title: GSEA
text:
B73-Y12 Figure reproduction
This mode works from previously stored DEP results rather than forcing the user to rebuild a separate expression/count input.

Load comparisons
Click LOAD PREVIOUS DEP RESULTS. You can select multiple DEP comparisons, Select all, Clear, or choose Root_VE only. A separate Focus comparison determines which selected comparison is displayed in detail.
The reproduction pathway is currently fixed to Phenylpropanoid biosynthesis for the archived target.


Root_VE reproduction source
Two sources are available:

Exact supplied figure (historical Root_VE) — default exact target;
Recalculate from loaded DEP result — rebuild the ranking from the selected stored comparison.

The frozen historical Root_VE target records 11,049 ranked proteins, 196 map00940 hits, the historical B73 − Y12 log2FC metric, and weighted GSEA p = 1. It is bundled specifically to match the supplied historical panel.
When recalculating from stored DEP, the ranking metric can be:

moderated t statistic (script method);
log2 fold change;
signed -log10(P-value).

Protein inclusion can use all tested proteins (the GSEA default) or custom thresholds.






WarningKeep comparison direction consistent



Changing B73−Y12 to Y12−B73 reverses the ranked statistic and therefore the enrichment direction. Record the comparison direction and ranking metric with every exported GSEA figure.

title: GSEA
text:
Outputs
Both modes provide ranked-pathway results and pathway-level visualization/export. In reproduction mode, selected comparisons can be recalculated while Root_VE can remain locked to the exact historical archive when exact panel reproduction is required.
Use standard mode for new general-purpose GSEA; use archived mode only when the historical B73/Y12 figure is the explicit target.

Recommended DEP is now the default
The current DEP module no longer treats an imputed normalized matrix as the default inferential input. Recommended DEP uses the observed Step4 log2 matrix, optional sample median centering, a detection filter, robust trend limma statistics and BH FDR control. An Archived reproduction mode remains available when historical figures/settings must be reproduced exactly. Additional comparison engines include DEqMS, proDA and MSstats when their required inputs are available.

PTM-aware annotation
For modified peptides, the explorer calculates theoretical b/y fragments with modification masses included and matches observed peaks within the configured tolerance. The Vac14 benchmark also includes neutral-loss candidates relevant to phosphopeptide fragmentation.
A convincing annotated spectrum supports identification confidence, but it does not establish quantitative significance across biological replicates.

title: PSM Explorer
text:
What to verify
Before using a spectrum in a manuscript, check the modified sequence/site position, precursor charge and m/z, spectrum/run identifier, matched b/y series, mass tolerance, and whether the modification is truly localized.






Warning



Do not interpret a PTM site as uniquely localized when the underlying search result does not provide site-localization evidence. Keep original PSM metadata with the exported spectrum.

Biological interpretation
A PTM abundance change can reflect modification occupancy, total-protein abundance, or both. Compare site/peptide evidence with protein-level abundance when possible.






Warning



Do not claim a unique modification site when the underlying search result does not localize the site confidently. Preserve the modified sequence, spectrum ID, precursor information and fragment evidence with the figure.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Use Multi-omics → Co-enrichment after enrichment analysis has been completed separately for multiple omics layers, contrasts, tissues, or protein clusters. The module compares enrichment results across two or three omics datasets, identifies shared and omics-specific pathways, and provides publication-oriented summary tables and plots.
The most important requirement is comparability: enrichment results should use compatible pathway identifiers, annotation versions, and biological backgrounds. A pathway appearing in only one layer can reflect true biology, but it can also arise from incompatible annotation systems or different background universes.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Co-enrichment interface
The screenshot below shows the current three-omics example with Transcriptome, Proteome, and Metabolome enrichment results. The interface contains Data Input, Column Mapping, Display Control, Color & Export, and Run & Download controls. The result area provides an overlap summary, source-data previews, a summary bar plot, a matrix-style UpSet plot, a significance bubble plot, and a table of shared/specific pathways.






Figure 1: ProtVis Co-enrichment interface showing a three-omics example with Transcriptome, Proteome and Metabolome enrichment results, overlap summary, UpSet-style overlap visualization and pathway significance outputs.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Choose two-omics or three-omics mode. Open Data Input and select Co-enrichment Mode. Use Two-omics when comparing two result sets and Three-omics when comparing three layers such as transcriptome, proteome and metabolome.
2. Name each omics layer. Set Omics 1 Name, Omics 2 Name, and, in three-omics mode, Omics 3 Name. These labels are propagated into summaries and plots, so use concise names that match the biological analysis.
3. Load enrichment results. Upload the enrichment file for each omics layer. ProtVis accepts .csv, .tsv, .txt, .xlsx, and .xls. For a quick demonstration, click Use built-in example data. The built-in example loads representative Transcriptome, Proteome and Metabolome enrichment tables; review the mappings and then run the analysis.
4. Set the adjusted p-value cutoff. The default Adjusted p-value cutoff is 0.05. Pathways are considered significant in each layer according to this threshold before shared/specific classifications are summarized.
5. Decide how duplicate pathway names are handled. Keep Remove duplicated pathway names within each omics selected unless there is a specific reason to preserve duplicate descriptions. This avoids counting the same pathway more than once inside one omics layer.
6. Verify Column Mapping. Open Column Mapping and, for each uploaded dataset, select the correct Pathway column and Adjusted p-value column. ProtVis attempts to guess these fields, but the selections should still be checked manually before running the comparison.
7. Configure Display Control. Choose Pathway Display Mode as All, Shared only, or Specific only. Use the group filter to focus on one overlap class when needed. Top N pathways in bubble plot controls how many pathways are shown in the bubble visualization; the current default is 20. The value-label and sorting options affect presentation rather than pathway classification.
8. Configure colors and export settings. Under Color & Export, customize colors for shared pathways, pairwise-shared pathways, and omics-specific groups. The UpSet active/inactive colors and bubble low/high colors can also be adjusted. Choose PDF or PNG for plot downloads; PNG export additionally uses the selected DPI.
9. Run the analysis. Open Run & Download and click Run. After processing, review the summary note above the overlap table to confirm the adjusted p-value cutoff, display mode, group filter, and Top N setting used for the current result.
10. Inspect the result panels. Overlap Summary reports the pathway classes and counts. Uploaded Data Preview lets you inspect the input enrichment tables. Summary Bar Plot compares class sizes, Matrix-style UpSet Plot shows overlap structure, Significance Bubble Plot summarizes pathway significance across layers, and Shared and Specific Pathways provides the underlying pathway-level table.
11. Export tables and plots. The Run & Download section provides downloadable two-omics and three-omics demo data, the summary table, the pathway table, and individual summary, UpSet, and bubble plots in the selected format.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Recommended input structure
Each omics enrichment file must contain at least a pathway/term field and an adjusted p-value field. Additional columns can be retained. A minimal example is:
Pathway,padj,Count
Carbon metabolism,0.003,28
Ribosome,0.018,35
Plant hormone signal transduction,0.021,19
Column names do not have to match this example exactly because they are assigned explicitly in Column Mapping.

title: Co-enrichment
section: How shared and specific pathways should be interpreted
text:
How shared and specific pathways should be interpreted
A pathway classified as shared is present among the significant enrichment results of more than one selected omics layer. A pathway classified as specific is significant only in the corresponding layer under the current cutoff. In three-omics mode, ProtVis can distinguish pathways shared by all three layers, pairwise-shared pathways, and pathways specific to one layer.
Do not interpret overlap alone as evidence that molecular changes occur in the same direction or involve the same genes/proteins/metabolites. Co-enrichment compares pathway-level enrichment membership; directionality and constituent features should be checked in the original differential and enrichment results.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Practical checks before interpretation
Confirm that all input tables use the same pathway naming/ID system, that enrichment backgrounds are biologically comparable, and that the adjusted p-values were calculated in a compatible way. If pathway descriptions differ only because of database-version naming changes, harmonize identifiers before upload.






Tip



For cross-omics comparisons, stable pathway identifiers are preferable to free-text descriptions whenever they are available. Descriptions can change between database releases even when the underlying pathway is the same.








Note



The pathways and counts shown in the screenshot belong to the built-in demonstration and are intended to illustrate the interface. Real results depend on the uploaded enrichment tables, column mappings, p-value cutoff, and display filters.

Peptide-centric evidence
When a peptide is associated with multiple functional assignments, the current peptide-centric workflow splits its intensity equally across those assignments before sample-level aggregation. This rule is explicit because shared peptides can otherwise inflate functional totals.






Warning



Protein groups and shared peptides create genuine ambiguity in metaproteomics. Taxonomic/function composition is only as specific as the upstream protein/peptide assignment. Preserve annotation and peptide mapping tables with the result.

title: Expression profile
text:
Use Multi-omics → Expression profile when the biological question concerns coordinated abundance trends across several samples, stages, tissues, genotypes or conditions rather than only one pairwise comparison. The current interface provides two complementary views: Kmeans trend clustering and a Heatmap trend-analysis mode.
The Kmeans workflow standardizes each feature across samples before clustering, so the resulting trajectories emphasize relative expression patterns rather than absolute protein abundance. Cluster membership can then be exported for downstream enrichment or network analyses.

title: Expression profile
text:
Expression profile interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current Kmeans interface using the bundled example data. The example contains 582 features × 8 samples and is clustered into six groups. The cluster sizes displayed in this particular run are Cluster1 = 64, Cluster2 = 169, Cluster3 = 115, Cluster4 = 105, Cluster5 = 56 and Cluster6 = 73; these counts are example-specific and will change with another matrix, sample order or number of centers.






Figure 1: ProtVis Expression profile Kmeans interface. The left panel provides CSV upload, Load built-in example, Download example CSV and method selection. The main Kmeans card contains Parameter, Run and Download controls plus Figure, Table and Input Data tabs. Six trend clusters are displayed for the built-in 582-feature by 8-sample example.

title: Expression profile
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Choose the input data. Upload an expression matrix as a .csv, or click Load built-in example to load the bundled kmeans.csv. The built-in file is not loaded automatically. After loading, confirm the green status message and inspect the Input Data tab before running clustering. The first column is used as the feature identifier and the remaining columns must be numeric sample values.
2. Download the example when preparing your own file. Click Download example CSV to obtain the same kmeans.csv used by ProtVis. This is the easiest way to confirm the required file structure before replacing the example values with your own protein-expression matrix.
3. Select the analysis method. Under Method, choose Kmeans for trend clusters or Heatmap for the heatmap-based trend view. The screenshot shows Kmeans selected.
4. Set the Kmeans parameters. Open Parameter. Choose the line color and set centers, which is the requested number of K-means clusters. The current default is 6. Use a biologically defensible value rather than increasing K only to make the figure appear more detailed.
5. Run Kmeans. Open Run and click Run. ProtVis standardizes each feature across the sample columns and then applies stats::kmeans() with the selected number of centers. The black line in each cluster panel represents the cluster-center trajectory, while the colored lines represent individual feature trajectories.
6. Review all three result tabs. Use Figure to inspect the trend panels, Table to review feature-to-cluster assignments, and Input Data to return to the matrix that generated the result. Check that the sample order on the x-axis follows the intended biological sequence; K-means does not infer chronological or treatment order for you.
7. Export the result. In Download, set the desired figure width and height, then download the Kmeans Figure as PDF and the cluster Table as CSV. Keep the cluster table when using cluster-specific protein sets for enrichment, annotation or network analysis.

title: Expression profile
text:
Input format
A suitable CSV has feature identifiers in the first column and numeric samples in the remaining columns, for example:
ID,Sample1,Sample2,Sample3,Sample4
Protein_A,10.2,12.4,18.7,21.1
Protein_B,30.5,24.2,17.9,11.6
Protein_C,8.1,14.6,13.9,20.4
ProtVis requires at least two sample columns, and all sample columns must be numeric. If samples represent an ordered experiment, arrange them in the intended chronological or biological order before clustering because that column order becomes the trend-plot x-axis.

title: Expression profile
text:
How Kmeans is calculated
For the Kmeans view, ProtVis scales each feature across samples before clustering. Conceptually, each row is transformed to a standardized trajectory and K-means then groups rows with similar shapes. This means a highly abundant protein and a low-abundance protein can enter the same cluster when their relative trajectories are similar.
The cluster title includes both the cluster number and the number of assigned features. In the bundled example shown above, six clusters contain a total of 582 features.






ImportantInterpret trend shape, not absolute abundance



Because Kmeans uses row-standardized values, the y-axis represents standardized relative change. Do not interpret the plotted y-value as the original protein intensity. Return to the original/normalized quantitative matrix when absolute abundance is required.

title: Expression profile
text:
Heatmap mode
Selecting Heatmap opens the Heatmap trend analysis (K-means) view. Set the number of K-means clusters and choose the scale mode: Row (trend), Column, or None. Run the heatmap and inspect the resulting cluster structure before exporting the cluster table.
Row scaling is appropriate when the goal is to emphasize within-protein trends across samples. Column scaling instead emphasizes sample-wise relative structure, while None retains the supplied numerical scale.

title: Expression profile
text:
Choosing the number of clusters
There is no universally correct K. Start with a moderate number, inspect cluster size and trajectory coherence, and compare nearby values when needed. Very large K values can fragment one coherent response into many small groups, whereas very small K values can merge distinct biological patterns.
A useful cluster should contain a recognizable trajectory and enough members to support the intended downstream interpretation. A cluster containing only a handful of proteins is not automatically wrong, but it deserves closer inspection before biological conclusions are drawn.

title: Expression profile
text:
Downstream use
Exported cluster assignments can be used to create cluster-specific protein lists for Enrichment analysis, pathway interpretation, PPI/network analysis, or other multi-omics modules. Preserve the sample order, preprocessing state, selected K and cluster table as part of the analysis record so that the trend analysis can be reproduced.






Note



Trend clustering is exploratory. Membership in a K-means cluster does not establish statistical significance for every protein in that cluster. Use DEP or an appropriate time-series/repeated-measures model when formal statistical inference is required.

Table-based input

  --input proteins.tsv \
  --source DIA-NN \

Use the source name that matches the input parser. The imported table is harmonized into ProtVis_dataset before later stages run.

title: Headless / CLI
text:
Reproducibility
A production CLI run should archive the command/configuration, ProtVis version and commit, input fingerprints, search-engine version, result registry, workflow status and portable ProtVis_dataset export.
Because schema v4 is append-only, re-running a stage adds a new run and preserves the earlier state instead of silently overwriting provenance.






Tip



Use the GUI for interactive exploration and the CLI for fixed, repeated production runs. Both routes operate on the same project model.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
ProtVis 0.9.1 uses both schema-v4 run history and serialized checkpoints/stage files. The active ProtVis_dataset is authoritative; checkpoints make that state recoverable, while the append-only run registry preserves earlier executions even when they are no longer current.






Figure 1: Checkpoint-aware analysis and recovery in ProtVis. Validated project states support resuming interrupted analyses and restarting from a selected stage.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Canonical checkpoint stages
The current ordered checkpoint progression is:
creation → import → noise_correction → transformation → imputation →
normalization → dimensionality_reduction → differential_analysis →
enrichment → network

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Save and list checkpoints
path <- save_protvis_checkpoint(
  dataset,
  directory = "checkpoints",
  stage = "normalization",
  keep = 20
)

list_protvis_checkpoints("checkpoints")
The listing reports path, stage, time, size, MD5 and readability. Checkpoints are written through a temporary file and validated before publication.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Restore the newest valid state
restored <- restore_protvis_checkpoint(
  "checkpoints",
  version = "latest"
)
or request a stage:
restored <- restore_protvis_checkpoint(
  "checkpoints",
  stage = "differential_analysis"
)
If the exact stage is absent, ProtVis can select the newest readable checkpoint at or before the requested stage.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Workflow invalidation
Schema v4 records dependency edges between runs. Re-running an upstream stage can invalidate its downstream dependants. Invalidated runs remain available in immutable history for auditability but should not be treated as current results.
Inspect the active/invalidated state in Project Dashboard, which exposes the run registry, workflow nodes and workflow edges.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Resume from the GUI
Use Project Dashboard → Resume workflow after reopening a project. Resume is state-aware: a Raw project that has not completed search is routed back to Search rather than being allowed to enter quantitative preprocessing.

Search recovery

Sage
A completed Sage project can be reconstructed from the project Sage_search context when lfq.tsv, configuration, FASTA and mzML inputs remain resolvable. Keep the whole directory together:
Sage_search/
├── sage_config.json
├── results.sage.tsv
├── lfq.tsv
└── results.json


FragPipe
FragPipe runs preserve the prepared workflow, manifest, runtime information, log and parsed result files under the project. The search run is also indexed by schema v4; keep the official workflow/runtime context with the project when reproducibility is required.

Portable export
export_dir <- export_protvis_dataset(
  dataset,
  directory = "ProtVis_release",
  include_raw = FALSE

A modern portable export can include the serialized dataset, matrices/metadata, annotations, process history, provenance, workflow status, result registry and per-run results/artifacts.






Tip



Keep the project directory, latest portable export, checkpoints and search directories together. This preserves both restartability and the evidence needed to explain exactly which run produced a final figure.

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
ProtVis is an R/Shiny proteomics platform that connects raw-data search, multi-source quantitative import, preprocessing, project QC, differential protein analysis, functional interpretation, multi-omics, PTM evidence and publication-ready visualization in one traceable workflow.
Install ProtVis · Start a project · Run Sage · Run FragPipe · Understand schema v4

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
ProtVis at a glance
The current workflow has two principal entry routes. Raw LC-MS data + FASTA enter through Search, where ProtVis provides Sage and FragPipe backends. Quantitative outputs from mainstream proteomics software or a user-defined matrix enter through source-specific import/parsing. Both routes converge on the same ProtVis_dataset schema v4.






Figure 1: Overview workflow in ProtVis. Raw LC-MS data and FASTA enter through database search, while mainstream proteomics software outputs and user-defined matrices enter through quantitative import. Both converge on ProtVis_dataset and continue through preprocessing, data summary, downstream analysis, multi-omics/WGCNA and key-protein characterization.





Dual Search backends

Use bundled Sage for lightweight FASTA + mzML search or integrated FragPipe headless workflows for broader DDA/DIA/PTM searches.



Multi-source import

MaxQuant, Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, Mascot, OpenMS and user-defined quantitative matrices converge on one data model.



ProtVis_dataset schema v4

Append-only run history, result registry, workflow graph, artifact index, assay registry, aligned metadata and structured provenance preserve the full analysis lineage.



Project Dashboard

Audit proteins/samples, completeness, CV, missingness, workflow state, input-file fingerprints and Sage/FragPipe search QC; resume from the latest valid node.



Recommended DEP

Analyze observed pre-imputation log2 intensities with detection filtering, median centering, robust limma/BH FDR, plus a separate presence/absence evidence stream.



Biological interpretation

Continue into GO/KEGG enrichment, directional KEGG, GSEA, Pathview, PPI, WGCNA, co-enrichment, metaproteomics and expression profiling.



PSM-level evidence

Use PSM Explorer to inspect Protein → Peptide → PSM → MS/MS evidence with PTM-aware theoretical fragments and annotated spectra.



GUI + CLI

The Shiny interface and run_protvis_cli() share the same project, search, checkpoint, provenance and export backend.

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
Recommended analysis paths
For vendor RAW data:
RAW → mzML when required → Project init → Search (Sage or FragPipe) → Project Dashboard → Pre-processing → Overview/QC → Recommended DEP → Interpretation
For already converted mzML + FASTA:
Project init → Search → Project Dashboard → Pre-processing → Overview/QC → Recommended DEP → Interpretation
For MaxQuant:
Project init → MaxQuant Output Preparation → Project Dashboard → Pre-processing → Overview/QC → Recommended DEP → Interpretation
For other tabular outputs, use the matching source parser and then enter the shared workflow.






ImportantRecommended DEP does not depend on imputed values



The current Recommended DEP workflow intentionally uses the observed Step4 log2 matrix before KNN/RF imputation, applies optional sample median centering and detection filtering, and keeps presence/absence candidates as a separate evidence stream. Imputation remains useful for visualization and analyses that explicitly require a complete matrix.

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
Reproducibility by design
Schema v4 keeps analysis executions as immutable runs. Core preprocessing runs preserve complete matrix snapshots; ordinary analyses preserve result tables, statistics, plot data/configuration, parameters, files and dependencies. Re-running an upstream step can invalidate dependent downstream nodes without deleting their historical runs.
Use Project Dashboard to inspect the active state, Checkpoints & recovery to resume safely, and Headless / CLI for automated production workflows.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
ProtVis_dataset is the canonical state container for the current application. It keeps the active quantitative matrix aligned with sample/protein metadata while preserving annotations, search evidence, analysis runs, artifacts, workflow dependencies and provenance.
The object does not inherit from mass_dataset. Legacy workspaces can be migrated where supported, but new analyses use ProtVis_dataset directly.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Schema v4 logical fields
Schema v4 keeps the S4 slot layout backward compatible while adding three project-wide logical structures:

result registry → metadata$result_registry;
workflow graph → metadata$workflow;
artifact index → metadata$artifacts.

The canonical immutable run store is:
dataset$analysis_results$v4$runs
Module-local/latest views are still available for compatibility, but they are mirrored into the append-only history rather than replacing previous runs.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Append-only analysis history
Every analysis execution receives a run ID and stores its method, category, status, parameters, tables/statistics/plot data, files and dependencies. Re-running a module does not delete the previous execution.
Core matrix-changing modules—noise correction, transformation, imputation and normalization—retain complete matrix snapshots with aligned metadata. Ordinary analyses retain their results and plotting/statistical context without duplicating the entire active matrix.
Useful APIs:
protvis_result_registry(dataset)
protvis_latest_result(dataset, "normalization")
protvis_result_history(dataset, "normalization")
protvis_result(dataset, run_id)
To activate a historical preprocessing matrix:
dataset <- protvis_activate_result(dataset, run_id)
Custom extensions can append results with:
dataset <- record_protvis_output(
  dataset,
  module = "custom_analysis",
  tables = list(result = my_table),
  plot_data = list(volcano = volcano_df),
  parameters = list(method = "my_method")
)

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Workflow dependencies
The workflow graph records nodes and edges between upstream/downstream runs. Re-running an upstream stage can mark dependent downstream nodes as invalidated. Invalidated results remain in history for auditability but should not be treated as current evidence.
Use Project Dashboard to inspect the run registry, workflow nodes/edges and current state.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Assay registry
Search workflows can retain PSM- and peptide-level assays separately from the active protein matrix. This allows Sage/FragPipe evidence and PSM Explorer workflows to coexist with protein-level quantitation without forcing every evidence type into expression_data.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Create a project programmatically
library(ProtVis)

expr <- data.frame(
  S1 = c(10, 20, 30),
  S2 = c(12, 18, 33),
  row.names = c("P1", "P2", "P3")
)

samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S1", "S2"),
  group = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  row.names = c("S1", "S2")
)

ds <- create_protvis_dataset(
  expression_data = expr,
  sample_info = samples
)

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
QFeatures interoperability
Optional helpers as_QFeatures() and from_QFeatures() connect ProtVis with the Bioconductor QFeatures ecosystem when those packages are installed. The conversion is optional; ProtVis_dataset remains the primary GUI/project state.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Raw-search staging
A Raw project is a deliberate exception to the normal non-empty expression-matrix rule. Project init can create a search staging object before protein quantitation exists. Search finalizes the project once Sage LFQ or a compatible FragPipe protein report has been parsed.

title: ProtVis_dataset schema v4
text:
Compatibility checkpoints
Stage files such as Step1_project_init.rda through Step7_differential_analysis.rda remain useful for older workflows and recovery. They are compatibility snapshots, not the canonical run registry.






ImportantCurrent state versus history



expression_data points to the active matrix. Historical matrices/results remain available through the run registry. Always verify the active run/node before exporting a final figure or table.

title: Project Dashboard
text:
Project Dashboard is the project-wide audit page in ProtVis 0.9.1. Open it after Project init, database search or preprocessing to answer four questions: what data are active, whether the matrix is sufficiently complete, which runs are current/failed/invalidated, and where the project can safely resume.
The dashboard reads the active ProtVis_dataset; it does not create an alternative copy of the project.

title: Project Dashboard
text:
Top-level metrics
The summary cards report protein count, sample count, data completeness, median protein CV and completed workflow stages. A sample-level missing-value plot complements these project-wide metrics.
A staging Raw project can legitimately have zero proteins before database search. In that state, continue to Search rather than treating the empty expression matrix as a QC failure.

title: Project Dashboard
text:
Workflow state
The workflow card and tables use the schema-v4 dependency graph. Nodes can be complete, failed or invalidated. When an upstream step is re-run, downstream results that depend on the previous upstream state can be marked invalid instead of being presented as current.
A result can therefore remain in immutable history while no longer being valid for the currently activated data state.

title: Project Dashboard
text:
Resume workflow
Click Resume workflow to continue from the newest valid checkpoint/node. Resume is dependency-aware: a project in Sage_staging is sent back to Search rather than entering quantitative preprocessing without a real protein matrix.
If a node failed, inspect the recorded error and inputs before retrying. Re-running a node records a new run and preserves earlier failed/history entries.

title: Project Dashboard
text:
HTML report
Use HTML report to capture a portable QC snapshot of the project state. For publication or archiving, keep this report together with the exported ProtVis_dataset, workflow/status tables and result registry.

title: Project Dashboard
text:
Recommended review points
Open Project Dashboard after Project init, after Sage/FragPipe Search, after shared preprocessing, before final DEP/enrichment interpretation, and before project release.






Tip



The dashboard is an audit surface, not a replacement for module-specific plots. Use it to establish which data state and run are current, then interpret biological figures in their dedicated modules.

title: Multi-omics
text:
Schema-v4 behavior
Where a module is connected to the active ProtVis_dataset, a completed analysis is appended as a new run with parameters and result tables rather than overwriting previous output. This is especially important for Metaproteomics, which can load the active project and preserve taxonomy/function/peptide analysis in the same lineage.

title: Multi-omics
text:
Recommended practice
Use a multi-omics module only when the biological question genuinely requires integration. Keep identifiers harmonized across layers, preserve each layer’s original statistics, and do not interpret visual overlap as statistical evidence unless an explicit test supports it.

title: WGCNA
text:
The current WGCNA module provides a complete sequence from data filtering to network interpretation:
Data cleaning → Filtering → Soft threshold → Module detection → Trait association → Interested module → Hub gene/protein → Cytoscape export
Although some UI labels use “gene”, the module can analyze protein abundance matrices.

title: WGCNA
text:
The current WGCNA module provides a complete sequence from data filtering to network interpretation:
Data cleaning → Filtering → Soft threshold → Module detection → Trait association → Interested module → Hub gene/protein → Cytoscape export
Although some UI labels use “gene”, the module can analyze protein abundance matrices.

title: WGCNA
text:
Input
Upload a .txt, .tsv, or .csv expression matrix. The first column should contain feature IDs and the remaining columns should be samples. The format selector includes count, expected count, normalized count, peak area (metabolomics), and protein abundance.
Select an unsigned or signed network and the appropriate preprocessing/normalization mode for the supplied data.

title: WGCNA
text:
Filtering
The first filter removes low-abundance features based on sample percentage and expression cutoff. The second filter ranks variability using MAD or Variance and retains the requested number of features.
Filtering is especially important for proteomics because a network built from thousands of uninformative or extremely sparse proteins can be unstable and computationally expensive.

title: WGCNA
text:
Soft-threshold selection
Run the soft-threshold analysis, review the scale-free topology fit, and either use the recommended power or specify a justified custom power. The default target displayed by the UI is an \(R^2\) cutoff of 0.8.

title: WGCNA
text:
Module detection
Set minimum module size, module merge/cut-tree height, and maximum block size, then run module detection. Export the protein-to-module table so every downstream claim can be traced back to module membership.

title: WGCNA
text:
Trait association
Upload trait data and run module-trait analysis. Check sample names carefully: trait rows/columns must correspond to the same samples represented in the expression matrix.

title: WGCNA
text:
Hub proteins and Cytoscape
Select a trait and module, set absolute kME/GS cutoffs, and run hub analysis. ProtVis can generate node and edge tables for Cytoscape using a user-defined network-weight threshold.






Warning



WGCNA requires enough samples to estimate correlations meaningfully. Very small proteomics experiments can produce visually convincing but unstable networks. Treat network topology cautiously when sample size is limited.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Use Multi-omics → Nine quadrant to compare two quantitative effect estimates, most commonly matched log2FC values from two omics layers or two related contrasts. ProtVis divides the x- and y-axes with the same absolute fold-change cutoff and assigns every row to one of nine directional classes: Up/Up, Up/NS, Up/Down, NS/Up, NS/NS, NS/Down, Down/Up, Down/NS, and Down/Down.
This view is useful for separating concordant changes, discordant changes, and changes detected mainly in one omics layer.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Nine-quadrant interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current module with the bundled demonstration data. The built-in example contains 2,800 rows × 4 columns: Omic1_ID, Log2FC_Omic1, Omic2_ID, and Log2FC_Omic2. The quadrant counts visible in this run are example-specific and will change with another dataset or cutoff.






Figure 1: ProtVis Nine-quadrant interface using the built-in two-omics demonstration dataset. The left sidebar contains Data Input, Plot Settings, Color Settings and Download Settings. The center card previews the input table and the right card displays the nine-quadrant plot and quadrant-specific result panels.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load the data. Open Data Input and either upload a .csv/.xlsx file or click LOAD DEMO DATA. The demonstration dataset is not loaded automatically. Use Download example CSV when you want a template for preparing your own file.
2. Check the preview. The Uploaded Data Preview card should show the expected row and column counts. ProtVis requires at least two numeric columns for the plot.
3. Select the x- and y-axis variables. Choose the numeric field for Select Omic1 (X-axis) and the numeric field for Select Omic2 (Y-axis). In the built-in example these are Log2FC_Omic1 and Log2FC_Omic2.
4. Set the fold-change cutoff. Open Plot Settings and set Log2FC Cutoff. The current default is 1. ProtVis uses +cutoff and -cutoff on both axes: values above +cutoff are Up, values below -cutoff are Down, and values between the thresholds are NS.
5. Control quadrant labels. Keep Show Quadrant Counts selected if you want the number of rows in each of the nine regions to be displayed on the figure.
6. Run the plot. Click Run plot. The status badge changes to Ready when the classification and plot have been generated.
7. Inspect the biological direction classes. Up/Up and Down/Down represent concordant responses, whereas Up/Down and Down/Up represent opposite responses. Up/NS, Down/NS, NS/Up, and NS/Down indicate that only one selected layer crosses the fold-change threshold. NS/NS contains rows within the cutoff on both axes.
8. Inspect and export the quadrant tables. Below the plot, ProtVis creates expandable panels for all nine classes. Each panel contains the corresponding rows and provides an individual CSV download button, which is useful for taking a selected directional class into enrichment or network analysis.
9. Export the figure. Under Download Settings, set the PDF width and height and click Download PDF. The current defaults are 8 × 6 inches.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Input format
A minimal file can contain separate identifiers for the two layers and one numeric effect column for each layer:
Omic1_ID,Log2FC_Omic1,Omic2_ID,Log2FC_Omic2
Gene_001,1.52,Protein_001,1.18
Gene_002,-2.10,Protein_002,-1.43
Gene_003,0.35,Protein_003,1.76
The selected x- and y-axis columns must be numeric. Other columns can remain in the input and will be retained in the preview and exported quadrant tables.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Color settings
Open Color Settings to customize all nine classes independently: Up_Up, Down_Down, Up_Down, Down_Up, Up_NS, Down_NS, NS_Up, NS_Down, and NS_NS. Color changes affect presentation only; they do not change class membership.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Interpretation
The nine-quadrant module performs directional classification from the selected numeric values and cutoff. It is not a substitute for formal differential statistics. When available, perform the appropriate DEP/DEG analysis first and retain adjusted p-values or significance labels alongside the fold changes.






WarningKeep contrast direction consistent



If one layer uses Treatment - Control while the other uses Control - Treatment, biologically concordant responses will appear discordant. Verify contrast direction before interpreting the quadrant pattern.








Note



The built-in 2,800-row dataset is a demonstration dataset intended to show the interface and output structure. The quadrant counts in the screenshot are not expected values for real experiments.

title: Venn
text:
Use Multi-omics → Venn to compare membership across multiple gene, protein, phosphoprotein, metabolite, or other feature sets. The current ProtVis module supports both Venn and UpSet visualization from the same input table.
In Auto mode, ProtVis uses a Venn diagram when the dataset contains six or fewer sets and switches to an UpSet plot when there are more than six sets. You can also force Venn or UpSet manually when appropriate.
